outputs.L1:
**From the Mithridatic Wars, First Century BC**

Our general was elsewhere,  
but we drowned.

While he rested,  
he shipped us home  
with the bulk of his spoils  
that had weighed his army down.

The thrashing storm  
that caught us cracked the hulls  
and made us offerings to the sea floor—  
a rain of statues, gold, and men.

Released from service,  
done with war,  
the crash and hiss muted,  
we fell through streams of creatures  
whose lives were their purpose.

We settled with treasure looted  
from temples of rubbled Athenian Greece;  
among us, bronze and marble gods and goddesses,  
moored without grace,  
dodged by incurious fish.

Their power was never meant to buoy us—  
our pleasures were incidental gifts—  
but, shaken by their radiance in our dust,  
we had given them our voices.

Their faces, wings, and limbs  
lie here with our sanded bones  
and motionless devices.

Little crabs attempt to don rings  
set with agate and amethyst,  
and many an octopus,  
seeking an hour of rest,  
finds shelter in our brain-cases.

So we are still of use.
outputs.L2:
**The Mithridatic Wars, first century BC**

Our commander was far away  
when the sea took us.

While he recovered,  
he sent us back across the water,  
along with most of the plunder  
that had slowed his troops.

A violent tempest seized the ships,  
split their timbers,  
and scattered men, gold, and statues  
like tribute sinking to the seabed.

Our campaigns finished,  
our military duty ended,  
the roar of wreckage fading above,  
we descended among currents of animals  
that existed simply to live.

We came to rest beside riches  
stripped from the sanctuaries  
of ruined Greek Athens.  
Bronze and marble divinities  
were pinned clumsily to the bottom,  
while indifferent fish passed around them.

Those gods had no power  
intended to hold us above water;  
the delights they granted were only by-products.  
Yet their brilliance had startled us  
amid the dirt of life,  
and we had spoken on their behalf.

Now their features, feathers, and limbs  
remain beside our bones, polished by sand,  
and the useless mechanisms we carried.

Tiny crabs try on  
agate- and amethyst-studded rings.  
Many octopuses, searching for a brief refuge,  
curl inside our skulls.

Even now, then,  
we serve a purpose.
outputs.L3:
As soldiers returned home from the Mithridatic Wars, a violent storm overtook their ships and shattered them at sea. Men, statues, gold, and other treasures plundered from the temples of Greece were cast into the water and dragged down to the seafloor.

There, the bodies of the soldiers came to rest beside the bronze and marble images of the gods they had once worshipped. In life, the men had given these deities their voices, prayers, and reverence; in death, the powerless divine figures could do nothing to save them. Soldiers and statues lay together in silence, gradually disappearing beneath layers of sand and drifting dust.

Over time, the wreck became part of the marine world. Sea creatures moved among the scattered remains, turning the debris of conquest into shelter and ornament. Rings, skulls, broken statues, and other remnants of war now serve as hiding places and adornments for the creatures that inhabit the ruins.
outputs.L4:
The poem gives voice to soldiers who drowned during the Mithridatic Wars, allowing the dead to speak not as separate individuals but as a collective presence beneath the sea. From this underwater perspective, they recall the violence that brought them there: military conflict, shipwreck, death, and the loss of treasures seized in war. Weapons, ornaments, bodies, and sacred objects now lie together on the seabed, stripped of the distinctions they once carried. The sea has reduced conquerors and conquered, sacred and ordinary, human remains and valuable possessions to the same submerged condition.

This collective voice also reflects on the collapse of human and divine power. The soldiers’ deaths reveal the fragility of military glory, while the presence of fallen or powerless divinity suggests that even the gods and symbols used to justify war cannot escape ruin. Objects once valued for their beauty, wealth, or religious significance no longer serve their original purposes. Underwater, the hierarchies of the living world cease to matter: treasure cannot enrich its owners, armor cannot protect its wearers, and divine images can no longer command reverence.

Yet the poem does not end only in desolation. Its final image shows marine creatures inhabiting human remains and discarded ornaments. What was once a body becomes shelter; what was once decoration or treasure becomes part of a new environment. Nature does not preserve the former meanings of these objects, but neither does it leave them entirely useless. Instead, it absorbs and repurposes the ruins of violence.

The ending therefore combines grim irony with a form of renewal. Human ambition, warfare, wealth, and sacred authority have all been defeated, but the physical remains of that defeated world enter another cycle of life. The sea transforms the wreckage of history into habitat, restoring practical value to lives and objects that war had emptied of their former power. In doing so, the poem suggests that nature outlasts human conflict and quietly converts its ruins into the materials of continued existence.
outputs.L5:
## From the Mithridatic Wars to Roman Supremacy

The Mithridatic Wars were a series of three conflicts fought between the Roman Republic and Mithridates VI, the powerful king of Pontus, from 88 to 63 BCE. Mithridates sought to expand his influence across Asia Minor and weaken Roman control in the eastern Mediterranean. Presenting himself as a defender of Greek independence, he gained support among communities that resented Roman taxation and administration.

The First Mithridatic War began after Mithridates occupied several Roman-allied territories. His forces advanced into Greece, but Roman general Lucius Cornelius Sulla defeated them and compelled Mithridates to accept peace. The conflict soon resumed, however, as neither side was willing to abandon its ambitions.

During the Third Mithridatic War, Roman commanders Lucullus and Pompey gradually destroyed the king’s military power. Pompey’s victories forced Mithridates to flee to the region of the Black Sea, where he later died following a revolt led by his son.

Rome emerged from the Mithridatic Wars as the dominant power in Asia Minor and the eastern Mediterranean. The victories also strengthened Pompey’s political reputation and allowed Rome to reorganize large eastern territories into provinces and dependent kingdoms. Thus, the wars marked an important stage in Rome’s transformation from a regional republic into a vast imperial power.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem narrated collectively by Roman soldiers who drowned in a shipwreck during the Mithridatic Wars while transporting looted Greek treasure home.
counterfactuals.output:
We were Rome while the oars held.

Bronze at our belts,  
salt in the seams of our wounds,  
we crowded the transport  
with gods who had not consented:

Apollo without his hand,  
a marble Kore blind with lime,  
kraters nested like helmets,  
coins impressed with the face  
of a king we had failed to kill.

Behind us, Asia burned  
in several languages.

We had pried gold leaves  
from temple doors,  
rolled painted cloth around spear shafts,  
laughed at the little household gods  
wrapped in wool beneath the benches.

Home, we said.

Home was the word  
we gave the western horizon,  
where our wives waited  
or had ceased to wait,  
where the Forum would weigh our plunder  
and call its weight glory.

Then the sea revised us.

Wind tore the square sail  
into a legion of white rags.  
The mast went down  
like a standard in rout.  
Oars snapped.  
Amphorae broke open,  
pouring wine among our feet  
dark as arterial blood.

We bailed with shields.  
We prayed to Neptune,  
then to the Greek god of the sea,  
then to every stolen face  
rolling in the hold.

No answer—

unless thunder was an answer,  
unless the hull’s long cracking  
was judgment spoken slowly.

When the ship opened,  
treasure learned its true allegiance.

Silver sank first,  
quick and certain.  
Bronze followed.  
Marble drew us after it.

Some clung to statues  
as drowning men cling to comrades,  
but the gods were heavier  
than belief.

We went down together:  
veterans, boys, mule drivers,  
a centurion still shouting ranks  
into the green disorder.

Our red cloaks flowered once  
beneath the waves  
and closed.

Now we lie without formation  
among cups no one drinks from,  
helmets filling with sand,  
coins beyond all spending.

Fish enter the mouths  
of philosophers carved in stone.  
An octopus inhabits Athena’s shield.  
The king’s gold profile  
dims under coral.

Above us, empires continue  
their brief arrangements.

Merchants cross our weather.  
Generals rename victories.  
On distant roads, triumphs pass—  
laurel, trumpet, chained captives—  
and Rome believes  
what reaches Rome belongs to Rome.

But we, who carried Greece away  
and could not carry breath,  
know otherwise.

The sea keeps no spoils.

It makes one province  
of thief and treasure,  
one silence  
of the conquered and the conqueror.

We were Rome while the oars held.

Afterward,  
we were only men  
falling through the dark,  
our hands still closed  
around what was never ours.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an ekphrastic historical poem about an ancient Roman wreck carrying statues, gold, and soldiers to the seafloor, ending with crabs wearing jeweled rings and octopuses sheltering in human skulls.
counterfactuals.output:
**Cargo for Neptune**

On the mosaic sea, beneath a hammered sun,  
the emperor’s galley leaned into the wind,  
its bronze ram parting provinces of blue.  
Along the deck stood marble gods in rope—  
Apollo blindfolded with sailcloth,  
Venus boxed among amphorae of oil—  
while cedar chests, iron-clasped,  
kept the hard yellow silence of tribute.

Soldiers slept against their crimson shields,  
dreaming of Rome’s white stairs,  
of bread, applause, and girls at fountains.  
Their centurion watched the western clouds  
assemble like a barbarian host.  
No augur had read the gulls correctly.  
No priest had heard, beneath the oars,  
the sea rehearsing its verdict.

Night struck. The mast cracked like a spear.  
Rain erased the constellations;  
the hull opened its dark red mouth.  
Gold aurei scattered through the hold,  
each Caesar’s profile flashing once  
before the deep annulled his reign.

Down went the legionaries, mail-heavy,  
grasping at ropes, at gods, at one another.  
Down went Athena, calm in stone;  
down went the emperor’s gilded face;  
down went wine jars, helmets, dice,  
letters never carried home.  
The seabed received them without triumph,  
laying silt over rank and wound.

Centuries passed in green procession.  
Empires thinned to names on broken maps.  
The statues gathered coral crowns;  
eels threaded the ribs of the ship;  
coins slept beyond all commerce,  
bright beneath the patient sand.

And where Rome had stamped its seal on the world,  
crabs wore jeweled rings,  
and octopuses sheltered in human skulls.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine the victims of a first-century BC shipwreck speaking from beneath the sea. Their general survived elsewhere, but they sank alongside spoils taken from ruined Athenian temples. Write their eerie monologue in lyrical free verse.
counterfactuals.output:
We went down with the marble gods.

Above us, the sea closed  
like a blue eyelid,  
and daylight shattered  
into coins.

Sulla lived.

Far off, his red standards  
dried in the Italian wind;  
his name entered Rome  
wearing iron and laurel.

But we—  
rowers, guards, merchants,  
men whose names were never carved—  
kept faith with the plunder.

Athena’s broken gaze sank beside us.  
Her temples had smoked on the hill.  
Bronze hands reached through the dark,  
still asking for their spears.  
A youth of polished stone  
fell forever without striking the ground.

We heard amphorae crack  
like old bones.  
Gold whispered in its chests.  
The strange bronze wheel,  
crowded with tiny teeth and stars,  
continued its drowned reckoning:

moon into shadow,  
season into season,  
kingdom into silt.

Was it a curse?  
Ask the eels threading our ribs.  
Ask the coral fastening  
red crowns to the gods.  
Ask the waves, which remember nothing  
and return everything changed.

We had carried ruined Athens  
upon our backs—  
its altars, its beauty,  
the cold faces of immortals—  
bound westward for triumph.

No triumph came.

Only the long descent,  
only sand entering the mouths  
that had shouted orders,  
prayers, prices, names.

Sulla lived.

We say it still  
from beneath the island’s black water,  
where no herald hears us:

The general lived.  
The statues lived.  
Even the heavens lived  
inside their corroded machine.

Only we became  
the silence between them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a haunting poem inspired by the Antikythera shipwreck, blending war, plundered bronze and marble gods, marine life, human remains, and ancient mechanical devices. Use “we” as the narrative voice.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Wreck Remembers**

We went down carrying war in our mouths,  
salt in the wounds of the oarsmen,  
bronze gods chained beneath the deck,  
marble faces turned toward Rome.

We had taken them from burning sanctuaries—  
Apollo without his fingers,  
Herakles green with weather,  
a goddess whose empty eyes  
still accused the dark.

Then the sea rose like an army.

We broke upon Antikythera,  
timbers crying out, amphorae rolling  
like severed heads through the hold.  
Above us, men vanished into foam;  
below, the plundered immortals  
received them without mercy.

We became ribs among anchors,  
teeth in the silt,  
a wrist circled by a bronze coin  
no ferryman would accept.

Octopus entered the helmets.  
Eels threaded our cages of bone.  
Coral made kingdoms of our skulls,  
and fish, bright as little knives,  
fed where our names had been.

Still, in the ruined chest,  
the machine continued its silence—  
gears nested within gears,  
a bronze heaven counting  
the moon’s dark passages,  
the wandering stars,  
the appointed hour of eclipses.

We had built a hand  
to turn the universe.

We could not make it  
hold the ship together.

Centuries passed through us.  
The gods grew furred with salt.  
The mechanism clenched its green teeth.  
We dreamed of war above the water—  
new empires lifting old swords,  
new victors filling ships  
with the beautiful dead.

When divers descended,  
their lamps woke our darkness.  
They raised the youth of Antikythera,  
limb by bronze limb;  
they gathered marble divinities,  
cups, coins, the bones of the nameless,  
and the corroded clock of the sky.

But we remained in every fragment.

We are the hands behind the gears.  
We are the drowned beneath the gods.  
We are the conquered and the conquerors,  
tangled together in the weed.

Turn the mechanism.

Watch the planets return  
to their ancient positions.

The sea remembers the date  
of every war.

The sea predicts  
no end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, archaeologically informed prose poem in which drowned soldiers reflect on becoming useful again as part of a seabed ecosystem, surrounded by divine statues, treasure, fish, crabs, octopuses, and corroded technology.
counterfactuals.output:
We had been trained to become history quickly: a date stamped into a cartridge case, a unit number on a buckle, a telegram folded at the kitchen table. Instead the sea made archaeologists wait. It took our names first, then the paint from the helmets, then the sharp intentions from our rifles. Iron flowered into orange concretion. Bolts married plates. The engine room collapsed beneath a slow masonry of mussels, tube worms, and lime.

Around us the old gods lay in attitudes of interrupted command. A bronze Apollo, netted in fishing line, raised one green hand from the silt. Isis rested face-down among amphora necks. A marble emperor had lost his head but kept a shoal of anthias turning through the hollow of his cloak. Coins slept fused in black cakes; ingots bore stamps no living customs officer could read. Treasure, the divers called it, though the octopus preferred the silver bowl because it fit her body exactly.

We had once believed usefulness meant obedience. Now blennies nested in our magazines. Crabs entered through the eye sockets of gas masks and came out armored in rust. Conger eels occupied the torpedo tubes. A grouper hovered where the radio operator had listened for coordinates, its gills opening and closing like a signal no nation could decode.

The seabed catalogued us without pity: ceramic, bronze, lead, glass, bone; rivet, femur, compass, cup. Sand moved over everything in seasonal sentences. In the oxygen-poor mud, leather endured beside teeth. Above it, salt and current worried the wreck to lace. Our machine, designed to cross borders and break bodies, became relief in a level country—a reef by accident, a city by corrosion.

At night, plankton kindled over the guns. The statues seemed to remember worship, but perhaps it was only moonlight shifting through water. Apollo’s mouth filled with shrimp. Isis wore a crown of anemones. The emperor’s severed neck sheltered eggs.

We do not forgive the sea. We do not bless it. We speak from the dark utility of what remains: calcium returning to mouths, iron entering blood, cavities becoming nurseries. Once we were ordered to hold this position. At last we do.

Fish pass through our ribs. Crabs lift our buttons like small, astonished suns. The octopus gathers medals into her den, not knowing valor from any other bright obstruction. Above us, propellers bruise the water; sonar touches our ruined hull and withdraws.

We are useful again.

Not as soldiers.

As shelter. As mineral. As warning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
